newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FEATURE-Palestinians say Israeli taxes are weapon in Jerusalem.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Palestinians say Israeli taxes are weapon in Jerusalem.

text.p: Bankrupt and unable to pay his bills, Abu Tareq shut down his souvenir shop eight years ago and moved to a different field of work.
Last week, the middle-aged Palestinian from Jerusalem found himself haunted again by a huge Israeli tax bill on his defunct store.
"My store has been shut for eight years and now they are asking me to pay a quarter million shekels ($70,000) for the past two years," Abu Tareq said.
Abu Tareq is among scores of Palestinians in Arab East Jerusalem who have found themselves scurrying away from Israeli officials out to collect taxes under police escort.
Like the others, Abu Tareq believes stepped-up Israeli tax raids in June were part of a concerted pressure campaign by the Jewish state to drive out East Jerusalem's 160,000 Arabs.
"This is a silent deportation of Palestinians. An intensive, intentional campaign, similar to military schemes, against East Jerusalemites," said Abu Tareq.
His sentiment underscores deep Palestinian suspicions that Israel is trying to force them out in advance of future peace talks on the fate of the city claimed as capital by both sides.
Palestinians hope to raise their flag over East Jerusalem as capital of an independent state.
Israel, which occupied East Jerusalem in 1967 and later annexed it in a move unrecognised internationally, says it will never cede any part of the city.
The Israeli municipality of Jerusalem denied the recent tax raids were politically motivated.

"The Jerusalem municipality is conducting a campaign to clear debts for all Jerusalem residents...In the framework of this campaign, dozens of confiscations were made in the eastern and western parts of the city," the city said in a statement.
ISRAELI TAXMEN BACKED BY MACHINEGUNS
The commercial buzz of downtown East Jerusalem has been disrupted by shouting matches between Palestinian shopkeepers and Israeli taxmen escorted by police.

"The tax personnel enter with soldiers carrying machineguns without sending us any notices or warnings. They terrorise us by putting harsh economic constraints to force us to leave the city. This is ethnic cleansing," shopkeeper Abu Nabeel said.

He said he was forced to close down his clothing store after liquidation of his inventory was not enough to cover his income tax bill. He insisted Israel would never practice such procedures in Jewish West Jerusalem.

Merchants argue that the tax raids are aimed at undermining the already fragile Palestinian economy in Jerusalem, which has been hard hit by a continuous Israeli closure of the city -- the hub of Palestinian business -- from the West Bank.
Abu Nabeel said Palestinian merchants in the city were heavily indebted, "plus there is no cash in the city since it is isolated and West Bank customers cannot come in. We cannot pay the high taxes."
TRASH IN THE EAST, TREES IN THE WEST
Palestinians also complain they receive inadequate municipal services compared to those received in West Jerusalem.

In East Jerusalem's al-Thori neighbourhood, garbage lies uncollected and uneven streets are poorly lit. Just up the road, across the dividing between west and east, modern homes stretch along tidy, well-lit streets lined with trees.
"No taxation without services in East Jerusalem," shouted Ziyyad Hamouri, head of a Palestinian ad-hoc anti-tax action committee during a recent commercial strike in East Jerusalem.
Palestinian merchants in Jerusalem closed their shops on the final Sunday in June and took to the streets to protest the raids and lack of services.
But Olmert said he was unimpressed.
"I hear complaints from the east side and from the west side. No one likes to pay taxes, particularly people who think they have to pay a lot of taxes," Olmert said.
"They think if they can turn it and manipulate it into a political issue they can get away with it. No one will get away with it."
